title: Heliochat QBR - cost drivers + cache hit rate follow-ups
next_steps: Redwood (Nadia) to share a 2-week before/after export comparing cache hit rate, retries, and token out by route for Heliochat.
Heliochat (Sam) to test routing policy for /v1/chat/completions: move low-stakes support flows to llama-3.1-8b and keep escalations on 70b.
Redwood (Alex) to send best-practice doc links on prefix caching + prompt template stabilization and a short checklist for improving cache hit rate.
Heliochat (Priya) to confirm internal chargeback dimensions needed in CSV export (project vs environment) and preferred reporting cadence.
Schedule a 30-min technical session next week focused on cache key strategy and route normalization for Heliochat’s dynamic prompt fields.
transcript:
Meeting: Heliochat QBR - cost drivers + cache hit rate follow-ups
Date/time: 2026-02-03 09:00 PT (17:00 UTC)
Duration: 53 min
Attendees:
- Redwood Inference: Markus Klein (Solutions Eng), Nadia Rahman (Cost attribution), Alex Martinez (DevEx)
- Heliochat: Jordan Lee (Head of Eng), Priya Nair (FinOps), Sam Ortega (Staff ML Eng), Mina Park (Product)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Heliochat reviewed January spend drivers in Redwood Console Usage Insights beta.
- Largest drivers: token output growth on /v1/chat/completions, cache hit rate decline on the same route, and increased fallback/retry rate in EU region.
- Agreed to adjust model mix (70B vs 8B) for lower-risk flows and to stabilize prompts to improve prefix cache reuse.
- Redwood to provide export + a small playbook for diagnosing cache misses and retry-attribution.

Topics
1) Q4/Q1 usage recap and spend trend
2) Top cost drivers by route + model
3) Cache hit rate drop investigation (prompt changes, streaming, dynamic fields)
4) Model mix + routing policy options
5) Exports for finance + chargeback

Action items (verbatim)
- Nadia to send export and breakdown screenshots with the driver annotations.
- Sam to share a sample of the new prompt template and what parts are dynamic.
- Priya to list the columns needed for finance reporting and if they need “workspace/project” split.

Transcript

[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, cool. Folks can hear me okay?
[00:03] Jordan Lee: Yep.
[00:04] Priya Nair: Yeah, good.
[00:05] Sam Ortega: Yep.
[00:06] Markus Klein: Great. So this is our kind of QBR-ish review, mostly on usage and costs. We pulled the new Usage Insights view in the console. Nadia’s on, she owns the cost attribution pipeline. Alex is here too for docs and “what do I do next” kind of stuff.
[00:21] Mina Park: Hey.
[00:22] Markus Klein: Hi Mina.

[00:25] Markus Klein: Agenda-wise: quick trend for January, then top drivers, then we’ll talk about cache hit rate, and then model mix, because I know you all are thinking about which flows really need the 70B.

[00:38] Priya Nair: And exports, please.
[00:39] Markus Klein: Yep, exports too.

[00:42] Markus Klein: Cool. Let me share what we’re seeing. So in the console, Usage → Cost, we’re looking at last 30 days. Biggest line item is /v1/chat/completions on llama-3.1-70b.
[00:54] Jordan Lee: That tracks.

[00:56] Markus Klein: It’s about 68% of total inference spend for the workspace. Next is embeddings, which is stable, and then a smaller rerank route.
[01:06] Priya Nair: When you say “total”, it matches the invoice total? Like within rounding?
[01:10] Nadia Rahman: Yeah, for your account we’re within about 0.6% on the 30-day window. The drift is mostly timing—late events and a little rounding on token pricing.
[01:20] Priya Nair: Okay. That’s within my tolerance, but I need to be able to explain it.
[01:24] Nadia Rahman: Totally. We can include the “data freshness / partial window” banner and the export includes the as-of timestamp.

[01:33] Markus Klein: So the top drivers card—this is new in beta—calls out three things.
[01:38] Markus Klein: First: token out increased week-over-week. It’s saying +31% on output tokens for the main chat route.
[01:45] Sam Ortega: That’s probably the new “coach” responses. We made them more verbose.
[01:50] Mina Park: Yeah, we changed tone to be more detailed.
[01:52] Markus Klein: Yep. Second: cache hit rate dropped. It went from, I’m reading, 22% to 9%.
[02:00] Jordan Lee: Oof.
[02:01] Markus Klein: And third: retries/fallbacks increased in EU. That’s smaller but it’s not nothing.

[02:10] Jordan Lee: Can we unpack the cache thing first? Because we didn’t intentionally change caching.
[02:14] Nadia Rahman: Yeah. So just to level set, the metric in the insights view is “prefix cache hit rate” for your traffic. It’s derived from our runtime cache events, basically “was the prefix served from KV cache” for requests with sufficiently similar prompts.
[02:29] Sam Ortega: Similar meaning exact match or like fuzzy?
[02:31] Nadia Rahman: Exact on the tokenized prefix at the cache key boundary. So if you add a timestamp, a random UUID, even like “today is Tuesday” if that changes, it busts it.
[02:41] Sam Ortega: Okay. We added a dynamic “session recap” blob at the top. That might be it.
[02:46] Nadia Rahman: That would do it. Also, streaming changes can affect perceived overhead but not the cache key itself. The more common culprit is new dynamic fields.

[02:57] Markus Klein: Alex, do you want to jump in on the prompt stabilization guidance?
[03:00] Alex Martinez: Yeah. We’ve seen teams get big wins by freezing the system prompt and moving the dynamic bits later. Even if you need session metadata, you can append it after a stable prefix, so the stable part still hits cache. Also avoid “current time” strings unless you really need it.
[03:16] Mina Park: We put “current date” in the system message for compliance reasons.
[03:20] Alex Martinez: Got it. Sometimes you can move that into a tool call or a separate message that doesn’t break the longest shared prefix. But we should look at your exact template.

[03:32] Jordan Lee: The other thing: we introduced a new routing where some calls go through an OpenAI-compat endpoint. Does that matter?
[03:38] Nadia Rahman: For the cache itself, no; for attribution in the console, it changes the route dimension. But I think we’re mapping /v1/chat/completions and the compat route into the same normalized route for your workspace. If you see two rows, let me know.
[03:52] Sam Ortega: We did see two rows last week, then it merged.
[03:55] Nadia Rahman: That’s consistent with a normalization update we rolled out mid-month.

[04:02] Priya Nair: So the cache hit rate: if we fix that, what’s the dollar impact?
[04:06] Nadia Rahman: Roughly: on your 70B traffic, each cache miss costs extra prefill compute. You’re running a lot of long context. If we take hit rate from ~9% back to ~20%, you’d expect on the order of 8–12% reduction in total spend on that route, assuming token out stays constant.
[04:25] Priya Nair: That’s meaningful.

[04:28] Markus Klein: And the token out growth is separate. That’s just more generated tokens.
[04:33] Mina Park: Yeah we made the responses longer. But users like it.
[04:36] Jordan Lee: Users like it but finance doesn’t.
[04:38] Priya Nair: Correct.

[04:40] Markus Klein: (laughs) That’s the eternal tradeoff.

[04:43] Markus Klein: Let’s talk token out distribution. In the drilldown table, we’re seeing p50 completion length went from ~180 tokens to ~260. p90 is now like 900.
[04:55] Sam Ortega: That p90 scares me. What’s driving that? Hallucinated essays?
[04:59] Markus Klein: The “what changed” view flagged “max_tokens increased” on a subset of traffic.
[05:04] Mina Park: We increased max_tokens from 512 to 1024 for the coach mode.
[05:09] Jordan Lee: That explains it.

[05:12] Nadia Rahman: Also, retries: when a request times out or gets a transient 5xx, the retry can double count tokens if the model already emitted partial output. We attribute that separately as “retry overhead” in the breakdown.
[05:24] Sam Ortega: Is that the “streaming overhead” line?
[05:26] Nadia Rahman: Different. Streaming overhead is the protocol and chunking cost—small. Retry overhead is bigger.
[05:33] Jordan Lee: We did see some timeouts in EU.

[05:36] Markus Klein: Yeah. So on the route table, if we add region filter, EU-West has a higher retry rate, about 2.8% vs 0.9% in US.
[05:46] Sam Ortega: Any idea why?
[05:48] Nadia Rahman: Could be network path or local capacity. Also you had a few fallback events: 70B to a compatible 70B variant in a different pool. The model name in the console should show “fallback_model” in the drilldown.
[06:02] Sam Ortega: We saw something like “llama-3.1-70b-rt2” and didn’t recognize it.
[06:06] Markus Klein: Yep, that’s our internal variant for the same family, used for failover. It should be bucketed under the same “family” in reporting, but the raw model id may show in the export.
[06:17] Priya Nair: Please bucket it. Finance hates surprise line items.
[06:20] Nadia Rahman: Understood. In the beta, we’re improving the “model family/version bucketing”. I can make sure your export uses the “model_family” column.

[06:30] Markus Klein: Okay, next topic: model mix. Right now it looks like you’re using 70B for basically all chat flows.
[06:38] Mina Park: We wanted consistent quality.
[06:40] Jordan Lee: But we also have “simple FAQ” requests.
[06:42] Sam Ortega: And internal summarization.

[06:45] Markus Klein: Exactly. A common pattern is route-level or intent-level routing: 8B for short, low-stakes; 70B for complex or escalations. If you can get even 20–30% of traffic to 8B, the savings is large.
[06:59] Sam Ortega: What’s your recommendation? Is 8B good enough?
[07:02] Alex Martinez: For stuff like summarization, templated responses, routing, it’s usually fine. For complex multi-step reasoning, 70B is better. You can also do a two-stage: 8B first, and only escalate to 70B when confidence is low.
[07:16] Mina Park: We don’t have a confidence signal.
[07:18] Alex Martinez: You can use simple heuristics at first: user sentiment, number of turns, or “did we call tools”. Or even “if user asks for policy/legal, escalate”.

[07:29] Jordan Lee: We can do some of that. But what about latency? The 70B is already borderline.
[07:34] Markus Klein: 8B will help latency too. Also, if we fix cache hit rate, prefill latency drops.
[07:41] Sam Ortega: We’re also seeing long contexts. We’ve got like 12k tokens in some threads.
[07:46] Nadia Rahman: Yep, your context length distribution shows a meaningful tail. That tail is expensive and it also reduces caching effectiveness because fewer requests share prefixes.

[07:58] Priya Nair: Is there a way for us to set budgets? Like, alert when token out spikes?
[08:03] Markus Klein: In the console today, we can do usage alerts on spend thresholds. For the insights beta, we’re working on “what changed” weekly. Not email yet, but you can export weekly and ingest into your BI.
[08:15] Priya Nair: I’ll take CSV.

[08:18] Markus Klein: Great. On CSV: current export includes route, model family, model version, tokens in/out, cache hit/miss counts, retries, fallbacks, latency p50/p95, and cost.
[08:32] Priya Nair: Does it include project? We have two product lines.
[08:35] Nadia Rahman: If you split traffic by project/workspace on our side, yes. If it’s one workspace, you can use environment tag if you send it. Do you currently tag “project”?
[08:45] Jordan Lee: Not consistently.
[08:47] Sam Ortega: We tag “env=prod” and “env=staging”. Not project.
[08:51] Nadia Rahman: Okay. Then CSV will be at workspace + env. We can talk about adding a stable “project” tag in your SDK calls.

[09:02] Jordan Lee: Back to the cache hit rate: besides prompt stabilization, is there a Redwood setting we should flip?
[09:07] Nadia Rahman: Mostly it’s prompt behavior. There are runtime cache knobs but they’re usually not the blocker. One thing: if you are including user ids in the system prompt, that fragments the cache.
[09:16] Sam Ortega: We include a “user tier” string.
[09:19] Nadia Rahman: That’s fine if it’s low-cardinality. But if you include the literal user id, no.
[09:24] Sam Ortega: No user id.

[09:26] Alex Martinez: Another small one: avoid random ordering of JSON in tool schema text. We’ve seen that change tokenization enough to break prefixes.
[09:34] Sam Ortega: Interesting. We do embed a tool schema description.
[09:38] Alex Martinez: If it’s generated, make sure it’s stable across requests.

[09:44] Markus Klein: I want to make sure we cover the “top drivers” view itself. Priya, what do you need to report internally?
[09:51] Priya Nair: I need a narrative: “Spend went up because output tokens increased due to product change; cache hit rate fell due to prompt changes; and retries in EU created extra overhead.” Then I need a plan with owners.
[10:06] Markus Klein: Perfect. That’s exactly how we’d frame it.

[10:10] Jordan Lee: For retries: are you counting client retries or Redwood retries?
[10:14] Nadia Rahman: Both, sort of. We measure distinct request ids at the gateway and detect repeated attempts from the client. If a request is retried with same id, we attribute it as retry. If it’s a new id but same payload, we can’t always know.
[10:29] Jordan Lee: Okay, so we should fix our idempotency key usage.
[10:32] Nadia Rahman: Yes, that improves accuracy and reduces accidental double work.

[10:38] Sam Ortega: Can we see which route had retries? Is it just chat completions?
[10:43] Markus Klein: Mostly. Embeddings is low. Chat is where we see the spikes, and it’s mostly the streaming path.
[10:50] Sam Ortega: Streaming is required for our UX.
[10:52] Markus Klein: Totally. Streaming itself isn’t the problem; it’s that if the connection drops mid-stream, clients retry and you pay twice.

[11:03] Jordan Lee: So we should implement resume or stop retrying once some output is received.
[11:07] Alex Martinez: Exactly. Or a policy: if you got >N tokens, don’t retry automatically, show “tap to regenerate” instead.

[11:16] Mina Park: Product might accept that.

[11:19] Markus Klein: Cool. We can keep going, but I think we have the key items. Let’s do a quick recap and then decide next meeting.

[11:27] Markus Klein: Recap: spend drivers are token out growth from coach mode, cache hit rate drop likely from new dynamic recap block, and retries/fallbacks in EU.
[11:37] Markus Klein: Next steps: Sam will share prompt template; Nadia will send export and driver screenshot plus a “before/after” window; Alex will send docs on caching + prompt stabilization; Priya will confirm finance export columns and cadence; and we’ll book a technical session.

[11:53] Priya Nair: Can the export be automated?
[11:55] Markus Klein: Not scheduled emails yet. But you can call the export endpoint and drop it into Snowflake or whatever you’re using.
[12:02] Priya Nair: Okay. We can do that.

[12:06] Jordan Lee: Let’s schedule the technical session. Same group plus maybe one of our backend folks.
[12:10] Markus Klein: Sounds good. I’ll send times.

[12:14] Mina Park: Thanks.
[12:15] Sam Ortega: Thanks.
[12:16] Priya Nair: Thanks.
[12:17] Markus Klein: Thank you all.

(End of transcript. Note: Fireflies timestamping is approximate; speaker attribution may be imperfect in a few segments.)
